notes.body:
Think of a single lamp passed from hand to hand through the dark — that is what "it" is throughout this passage. The many names given to it — hidden knowledge, a deposit in the breasts of the righteous, the rule of the Judge, a thing with an outward and an inward — are not many things but **one thing seen from many sides**: the divine Knowledge (علم), the living Word (كلمة) whose origin is from Allah and which calls back to Allah.

Notice how the young man refuses to claim any speech as his own; he is only a follower of the right word. So when he tells of what Allah honored, protected, and concealed, he speaks of that same Word — the guidance placed inside creation and then **guarded**, so that clever schemers and proud thinkers cannot seize it by the force of their intellect.

This is why it wears two faces:

- Its outward (ظاهر) is the plain remembrance and proof — the verses anyone can hear and recite.
- Its inward (باطن) is "a sure drink," the deeper meaning that quenches only those who journey toward Allah.

The very same revelation is at once an open book for all and a hidden treasure for the few who truly seek it.

So who are its "rightful keepers"? Not the crowd, and not the merely lettered. They are **the righteous whom Allah trusts** — "a trust (أمانة) which they discharge and a bound which they do not exceed." In our Ismaili understanding these are the Friends of Allah (أولياء الله), the Imams and those they entrust, in whose breasts the Word is sheltered like light kept safe within a lamp. They do not invent it and they do not overstep it; they carry it faithfully and pass it onward.

And here is the tender point the passage leaves with us: this knowledge is guarded not to shut us out, but to draw us in. Seek knowledge, and we will come to know. The door is kept closed only so that we will learn to knock.
notes.anchor: and its secrets are guarded by those who are their rightful keepers
notes.quote: and its secrets are guarded by those who are their rightful keepers
etymology: علم (knowledge): from the root ع-ل-م, to mark or leave a sign. A landmark (عَلَم) is what guides a traveler across open land, so knowledge is the inner sign that lets the mind find its way to what is true.
ظاهر (outward): from the root ظ-ه-ر, the back or a hill's high ridge — what stands out and is plainly seen. It came to mean the surface of a thing, its open face on view to everyone.
باطن (inward): from the root ب-ط-ن, the belly or the interior of a thing. From the hidden inside of the body the word grew to mean any concealed depth lying beneath the visible surface.
أمانة (trust): from the root أ-م-ن, to be safe and secure. A trust is what you place into safe hands; the very same root gives faith (إيمان), the act of entrusting one's whole heart.
ولي (friend and guardian): from the root و-ل-ي, to be near with nothing in between. A walī is one drawn so close to Allah that no gap remains — at once a protector and a devoted, loving friend.

notes.body:
Allah did not make the mind full and finished. He made it empty on purpose, and that emptiness is not a flaw but an engine. A lack is a kind of pull: the very thing we do not have is what draws us toward it. **To be given a need is already to be pointed at its answer.**

Think of hunger. We come to the table not because we are full but because we are empty, and the emptiness is what moves our feet. Thirst is the same — the dryness drives us to water. The chapter leans on exactly this picture when it speaks of watering places for those who journey and a sure drink for those who seek. The seeking is not something added onto the thirst; the thirst *is* the seeking.

Two lacks are named here, and each drives its own search:

- ignorance (جهل) — not knowing pushes the mind toward knowledge (علم),
- want (فقر) — not having pushes the soul toward capacity and completion.

So when the passage says Allah compelled minds by ignorance and by want, the compulsion is gentle, not violent. He did not shout an order to seek from the outside; He built the seeking into us by leaving us short. **The hole in us is the map to what fills it.**

That is why the chapter's opening line carries a quiet promise — whoever seeks a thing is on the verge of finding it. To feel our own lack is not to have been abandoned. It is to have been aimed, lovingly, at the One who alone completes us.

notes.quote: by ignorance and by want, He compelled minds to seek knowledge and capacity
etymology: جهل (ignorance): from the root ج-ه-ل, to be ignorant. The same root also carries the sense of rashness and acting hastily, because one who does not know still rushes to act — so the word names not only the empty space of not-knowing but the restless push out of it toward علم.

فقر (want): from the root ف-ق-ر, tied to فَقَار, the bones of the spine. Poverty is felt as a break in the backbone; the needy one is bent by his lack. The word carries the picture of someone bowed low, leaning toward whatever will support and straighten him again.

علم (knowledge): from the root ع-ل-م, to know, kin to عَلامة, a mark or sign. To know is to read something by its marks. The chapter speaks of signs that point to Allah, so this knowing is exactly that — recognizing Him through the signs He set for those who look.
